prompt: What does the problem/solution/architecture/demo README structure stand for?
choices: Problem, Solution, Architecture, Demo
Intro, Install, Usage, License
Title, Badges, Table of Contents, Contributing
Overview, API Reference, FAQ, Changelog

prompt: Building on the Tier 0 'rowcheck' example, what should a README's first screen let a stranger do within about 30 seconds?
choices: Understand what the project does, why it exists, and how to run it
Read the entire Architecture section in detail
Review the full git commit history
Memorize every CLI flag the tool supports

prompt: Why doesn't a static code listing prove a project actually works?
choices: Code that reads correctly can still fail to run, mishandle real input, or not produce the claimed output -- nothing about reading source demonstrates execution
Code listings are always too long for a README
Markdown doesn't support code blocks
Reviewers never read source code at all

prompt: Which piece of evidence most directly proves a CLI tool runs and produces real output?
choices: A screenshot or GIF of an actual terminal session showing the command invoked and its real output
A UML diagram of the project's classes
A bulleted list of planned features
A badge claiming '100% tested'

prompt: Which sentence is documentation rather than marketing?
choices: Exits with code 1 and prints the row number, column, and failing rule when validation fails.
Blazing-fast, enterprise-grade validation trusted by developers everywhere.
The most powerful CSV validator ever built.
A revolutionary, best-in-class data tool.

prompt: A README claims a tool 'handles millions of rows in milliseconds' with no benchmark numbers or methodology attached. What does this module say is the likely effect on a technical reader?
choices: They start distrusting the README's other claims too, because an unverifiable superlative reads as marketing rather than documentation
They immediately deploy the tool to production
They assume the real number must be even higher
They skip evaluation and download it right away

prompt: In the problem/solution/architecture/demo structure, what belongs in the Architecture section?
choices: A short explanation of the key files or modules and how data flows between them, not the full source code
The complete source code of every file in the project
A list of every past contributor
The project's elevator pitch for investors

prompt: Why does this module say even a full four-part README still needs a short 'first screen' at the very top?
choices: Because most readers decide whether to keep reading within the first screen, the same lesson as the Tier 0 rowcheck rewrite -- the full structure serves the reader who keeps going, but the top still has to survive a 30-second skim
Because GitHub enforces a minimum README length
Because a license section is legally required to appear first
Because Architecture sections cannot be written without a summary above them
